cls: Farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist - modified bile acid
pharm: Selective agonist of the farnesoid X receptor that regulates bile acid synthesis and transport; used in primary biliary cholangitis
quick: 5 mg once daily; may increase to 10 mg after 3 months
With or without food; separate from bile acid sequestrants
Limited data; use only if needed
Reduced dosing in Child-Pugh B/C; contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis
LFTs, signs of decompensation, pruritus, lipids
summary: Obeticholic acid is a potent, selective farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist used, in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid or as monotherapy, for primary biliary cholangitis in adults with inadequate response to or intolerance of ursodeoxycholic acid. It reduces bile acid synthesis and hepatocyte bile acid exposure. It carries a boxed warning for hepatic decompensation and liver failure when dosed incorrectly in patients with advanced (decompensated) cirrhosis, and it is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis and complete biliary obstruction. Dose-dependent pruritus is the most common adverse effect, and dosing must be reduced in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment.
indications: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in adults with inadequate response to UDCA
Primary biliary cholangitis as monotherapy in adults unable to tolerate UDCA

dosage.d: 5 mg once daily; if adequate reduction in ALP/bilirubin not achieved after 3 months and tolerated, increase to 10 mg once daily

dosage.c: PBC - moderate to severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B or C)
dosage.d: Starting 5 mg once weekly; may titrate to 5 mg twice weekly (>=3 days apart), then up to 10 mg twice weekly based on response and tolerability

admin: Take once daily (or per the reduced schedule for hepatic impairment), with or without food
If taking a bile acid sequestrant, take obeticholic acid at least 4 hours before or after it
Correctly classify the patient's hepatic status before and during therapy to avoid overdosing
Manage pruritus with dose reduction, antihistamines or bile acid sequestrants as needed
moa: A semisynthetic analog of the bile acid chenodeoxycholic acid that potently agonizes the nuclear farnesoid X receptor (FXR). FXR activation suppresses bile acid synthesis (via reduced CYP7A1), decreases hepatocyte bile acid uptake and increases bile acid efflux, lowering intrahepatic bile acid concentrations and exerting choleretic and anti-cholestatic effects.

absolute: Decompensated cirrhosis (e.g. Child-Pugh B or C) or a prior decompensation event
Compensated cirrhosis with evidence of portal hypertension

preg: Limited human data; insufficient to assess drug-associated risk. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk.
lact: No data on presence in human milk or effects on the infant; because of potential serious effects, avoid breastfeeding or discontinue the drug, weighing the importance of treatment to the mother.
renal: No dose adjustment is required for renal impairment.
hepatic: Reduce dosing frequency in moderate to severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B or C) because of drug accumulation. Contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis or with portal hypertension; monitor closely and discontinue if decompensation occurs.

major: Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) - reduced absorption; separate dosing by >=4 hours
Warfarin - decreased INR; monitor and adjust
moderate: CYP1A2 substrates with narrow therapeutic index (e.g. theophylline, tizanidine) - increased exposure
Other drugs affecting hepatic function - additive risk
minor: Inhibitors of hepatic bile acid transporters - theoretical interaction
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol given underlying liver disease
interactions.diagnostics: May reduce HDL cholesterol and alter liver enzyme and bilirubin values used for monitoring

serious: Hepatic decompensation and liver failure (especially with incorrect dosing in advanced cirrhosis)
rare: Hepatic failure requiring transplantation or fatal outcome
emergency: Hepatic decompensation (ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, jaundice)

monitoring: Liver tests (ALP, total bilirubin, transaminases) at baseline and regularly
Signs/symptoms of hepatic decompensation and portal hypertension
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed; the schedule differs if you have more advanced liver disease
Report worsening tiredness, yellowing of the skin/eyes, abdominal swelling, confusion or black stools immediately
Itching is common; tell your doctor, as the dose can be adjusted or itch treated
If you take a cholesterol-binding (bile acid sequestrant) medicine, separate it from this drug by at least 4 hours
Keep all liver-monitoring blood test appointments
Tell your doctor if you take warfarin
pk: Biochemical (ALP/bilirubin) improvement over weeks to months
Effective enterohepatic recycling; conjugates persist (dose reduced in hepatic impairment)
Once-daily dosing (reduced frequency in hepatic impairment)
pearls: Boxed warning: hepatic decompensation and liver failure with incorrect (too frequent) dosing in advanced PBC/cirrhosis
Contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis and in compensated cirrhosis with portal hypertension
Dose-dependent pruritus is the most common adverse effect and a frequent reason for discontinuation
Reduce dosing frequency to weekly/twice-weekly in Child-Pugh B or C
Separate from bile acid sequestrants by at least 4 hours
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered on the same day; if it is nearly time for the next scheduled dose, skip it. For reduced (weekly/twice-weekly) regimens, follow the prescriber's instructions and do not take extra doses.
overdose: Overdose is associated with an increased risk of hepatic adverse reactions, including decompensation and liver failure. There is no specific antidote; observe and provide supportive care, monitor liver function and signs of decompensation, and discontinue the drug.
